title: Scientific uncertainty and quantitative risk assessment
shortTitle: Scientific uncertainty and quantitative risk assessment
summary: The Benzene notes explain why regulatory risk assessment combines incomplete empirical evidence with assumptions and policy judgment.
notes:
Evidence that a substance increases cancer incidence at high exposures may not establish the risk at lower current exposures. Long latency can make direct observation impractical. A dose-response curve projects relationships between exposure and harm, but constructing it may require assumptions about thresholds, animal-to-human differences, background illness, actual exposure, and interactions among substances. The supplied discussion notes that benzene experiments and exposure data did not provide a complete empirical answer. (Printed 985.)

The authors describe quantitative risk assessment as a continuing tool because regulators need decisions despite uncertainty and lack better alternatives. They characterize Benzene as making the method effectively obligatory in later health-regulation disputes. The question then often becomes whether a particular assessment is plausible, adequately supported, and reasonably explained. Their cited Hodgson and American Petroleum Institute decisions recognize the role of policy judgment at the limits of scientific knowledge while retaining review for arbitrary or capricious action. (Printed 985–986.)

This reading supports a distinction between statutory authority, required findings, evidence, and policy choice. A court may independently determine that the statute requires a finding of significant risk, while assessing the agency’s technical judgment through the appropriate review framework. Uncertainty does not itself prove either that regulation is legally forbidden or that any protective measure is authorized. The assigned material leaves the reader to explain the relationship among authority, evidence, and reasoned judgment in the particular statutory program.
